Panama Oil & Gas Output Disrupted as Dengue Outbreak Hits Workforce

A surge in dengue fever cases among employees at several oil and gas production sites in Panama has forced operators to curtail output, raising concerns over supply disruptions and project delays in the region. The outbreak, first detected at the start of June along the country's northern coast, has now affected an estimated 17% of the sector's workforce, according to the Panamanian Oil & Gas Producers Association (POGPA).

"Over 200 workers have tested positive for dengue in the past two weeks, prompting us to implement emergency health protocols and reduce the number of active crews," said Lucia Ortega, spokesperson for Petroluna S.A., one of Panama’s largest upstream operators. "We are prioritizing the safety of our employees, but this inevitably impacts production volumes."

Industry sources report that at least four major onshore and offshore sites have scaled back operations, with daily crude output estimated to be down by nearly 15%. The sector, which contributes approximately $1.6 billion annually to Panama’s economy, relies heavily on manual labor for site maintenance and drilling activities—functions now hampered by widespread absenteeism and quarantine measures.

Local unions have voiced concern over working conditions, citing inadequate mosquito control and limited access to medical facilities at remote installations. "Many of our members are being asked to work double shifts to maintain essential operations, despite the elevated health risks," said Juan Carlos Ibáñez, secretary-general of the National Oil Workers’ Federation.

POGPA has called for urgent government assistance to bolster medical teams and vector control efforts at affected sites. "Failure to contain the outbreak could lead to prolonged shutdowns and further economic losses for the industry," warned POGPA president Marta Villalobos.

Government health officials confirmed they are coordinating with site operators to distribute mosquito nets, conduct fumigation, and expedite medical care for infected workers. However, with the rainy season intensifying, experts say it may take several weeks before the outbreak subsides and normal production resumes.

As of press time, no timeline has been provided for the full restoration of operations.
